guide.title: Upper East Side, Manhattan: Farmland to Museum Mile
guide.intro: Before Fifth Avenue's mansions, the Upper East Side was farmland crossed by the Boston Post Road and, from 1837, the New York and Harlem Railroad, with Lenape fishing camps once dotting the East River shore. The neighborhood's transformation began after the Park Avenue railroad tunnel was covered in 1910, when industrialists including Andrew Carnegie and Henry Clay Frick built mansions along Fifth Avenue; the first apartment house to replace one of them was 907 Fifth Avenue, completed in 1916 at 72nd Street. That corridor became "Museum Mile," the stretch of Fifth Avenue between 82nd and 105th Streets now lined with the Metropolitan Museum of Art, the Guggenheim, and the Jewish Museum. To the east, Yorkville became a predominantly German enclave from 1880 onward, swelled further after the 1904 General Slocum disaster killed over a thousand Lower East Side Germans, sending survivors uptown.

sections.heading: Mansions to Museum Mile
sections.body: Before the Gilded Age, the Upper East Side was farmland traversed by the Boston Post Road and, from 1837, the New York and Harlem Railroad; Lenape fishing camps are thought to have once dotted the East River shore. The mansion era took off after the Park Avenue railroad tunnel was covered in 1910, drawing industrialists such as Andrew Carnegie and Henry Clay Frick to build along Fifth Avenue. As the private-mansion era waned, 907 Fifth Avenue, completed in 1916 at 72nd Street, became the first apartment house to replace one of them. The stretch of Fifth Avenue between 82nd and 105th Streets — Museum Mile — grew around institutions including the Metropolitan Museum of Art (founded 1870) and the Guggenheim (dedicated 1959), Frank Lloyd Wright's only museum design.

sections.heading: A German Enclave to the East
sections.body: Yorkville, the neighborhood's eastern section, became predominantly German from 1880 onward. The General Slocum steamship disaster of June 15, 1904, in which an estimated 1,021 of the 1,342 people aboard died — most of them German immigrants from the Lower East Side — accelerated the community's move uptown, and Yorkville went on to draw Czech, Slovak, Irish, Polish, and Hungarian immigrants as well.

sections.heading: Getting there by subway
sections.body: The Upper East Side is served by two trunk lines: the Lexington Avenue Line (4/5/6) running the length of the neighborhood, and the Second Avenue Subway, whose first phase opened January 1, 2017, with stations at 72nd, 86th, and 96th Streets served by the Q at all times plus limited rush-hour N and R trains. Rule of thumb: use the 4/5/6 for the west side of the neighborhood and Museum Mile, and the Q on Second Avenue for the eastern blocks toward Yorkville.

faq.question: How do I get to the Upper East Side by subway?
faq.answer: Use the 4/5/6 Lexington Avenue Line for the west side of the neighborhood and Museum Mile, or the Second Avenue Subway's Q train (plus limited rush-hour N and R) at 72nd, 86th, and 96th Streets for the eastern blocks toward Yorkville.

faq.question: What is Museum Mile?
faq.answer: It's the stretch of Fifth Avenue between 82nd and 105th Streets, lined with major institutions including the Metropolitan Museum of Art, the Solomon R. Guggenheim Museum, and the Jewish Museum.

faq.question: When did the Second Avenue Subway open?
faq.answer: Phase 1 opened January 1, 2017, with three Upper East Side stations at 72nd, 86th, and 96th Streets built for $4.45 billion. A Phase 2 extension toward Harlem-125th Street is under construction, with cost estimates ranging from about $6 billion to $7.7 billion.

faq.question: Is Central Park part of the Upper East Side?
faq.answer: Central Park borders the Upper East Side to the west; it is documented as a place within the neighboring Upper West Side guide.

faq.question: Where can I stay on the Upper East Side?
faq.answer: The Mark, the only New York City hotel named among The World's 50 Best Hotels, and The Carlyle, home to Bemelmans Bar and Cafe Carlyle, are both verified in-neighborhood options.

places.name: The Metropolitan Museum of Art
places.summary: Founded April 13, 1870, the largest art museum in the Americas, spanning roughly 2 million square feet with about 1.5 million works across 17 curatorial departments; recorded 5,727,258 visitors in fiscal year 2025, anchoring "Museum Mile" on Fifth Avenue.

photos.title: The Metropolitan Museum of Art
photos.description: The Fifth Avenue facade of the Metropolitan Museum of Art.
photos.author: Epicgenius

places.name: The Frick Collection
places.summary: Housed in industrialist Henry Clay Frick's Fifth Avenue mansion, with galleries that use minimal wall labels to preserve the domestic atmosphere; open Wednesday through Monday, 10:30 a.m. to 5:30 p.m. (closed Tuesdays), with pay-what-you-wish Wednesday afternoons.

places.name: Solomon R. Guggenheim Museum
places.address: 1071 Fifth Avenue (between 88th and 89th Streets), New York, NY
places.summary: Frank Lloyd Wright's only museum design, dedicated October 21, 1959, famous for its six-story helical ramp gallery under a central skylight; drew nearly 861,000 visitors in 2023.

photos.title: Solomon R. Guggenheim Museum
photos.description: Frank Lloyd Wright's rotunda exterior seen from Fifth Avenue.
photos.author: Ajay Suresh

places.name: Lexington Candy Shop
places.address: 1226 Lexington Avenue at 83rd Street, New York, NY 10028
places.summary: A classic luncheonette and soda fountain founded in 1925, celebrating its 100th anniversary in 2025 as, by its own description, NYC's last reminder of the neighborhood soda-fountain era.

places.name: Daniel
places.summary: Daniel Boulud's flagship French restaurant, Michelin Guide-recognized and a member of Les Grandes Tables du Monde and Relais & Chateaux.

places.name: Orwashers Bakery
places.summary: Founded in 1916 by Hungarian immigrants to bake traditional rye, black, and grain breads, one of New York's oldest bakeries; its original Upper East Side storefront remains open.

places.name: Papaya King
places.summary: The iconic hot-dog-and-papaya-drink stand that originated on East 86th Street; after its original building was sold for redevelopment, it reopened half a block away on July 6, 2024.

places.name: The Mark
places.address: Madison Avenue at 77th Street, New York, NY 10075
places.summary: A luxury hotel with interiors by Jacques Grange and The Mark Restaurant by Jean-Georges; the only New York City hotel named among The World's 50 Best Hotels.

places.name: The Carlyle, A Rosewood Hotel
places.summary: A storied Upper East Side hotel home to Bemelmans Bar, with murals by Madeline author Ludwig Bemelmans, and Cafe Carlyle, a supper club currently in its 70th-anniversary season.
